FINAL TERM PAST SOLVED SUBJECTIVE QUESTIONS

   BT406 Research Methodology & Skill Enhancement

   SOJHLA FATIMA                37 - QUESTIONS          31-08-2020

1. Define historiography?
Historiography is the study of the methods of historians in developing
history as an academic discipline, and by extension is anybody of historical
work on a particular subject.
2. Explain validity of secondary data?
Secondary data generally have a pre-established degree of validity and
reliability which need not be re-examined by the researcher who is re-using
such data. ... Secondary data can provide a baseline for primary research to
compare the collected primary data results to and it can also be helpful in
research design.
3. How can we categorized descriptive statistics give example?
Descriptive statistics are brief descriptive coefficients that summarize a
given data set, which can be either a representation of the entire or a
sample of a population. Descriptive statistics are broken down into
measures of central tendency and measures of variability (spread). For
example, it would not be useful to know that all of the participants in our
example wore blue shoes. ... Central tendency describes the central point in
a data set. Variability describes the spread of the data
4. Different qualitative and quantitative research with example?
Qualitative research
To gain an in-depth understanding and explanation of some particular social
phenomenon
The data collection is done by interviewing; however, an understanding of
the social phenomenon and personal lived experiences of individuals might
be gained via non-intrusive qualitative approaches in which there searcher
might use texts, journals, written narratives or observations.
Quantitative research
Quantitative research, on the other hand, explores descriptive analysis of
characteristics through variables or answers questions about the
relationships among variables.
5. Emnurate the part of main body of reseach report?

1. Introduction 2. Background 3. Objectives 4. Methodology.
6. What points should one keep in mind while putting other research work
done in table?
I.Give each table a number.
II. Give each table a title.
III. Label the row and column variables, and give name to each of the
variable categories.
IV. Include the totals of the columns and rows. These are called as
marginal.
V. Each number or place that corresponds to the intersection of category for
each variable is cell of a table.
VI. Missing information to be given under the table
7. What is running record?
Files or existing statistical documents maintained by organizations. Vital
statistics.
8. Explain participant and non-participant observation study?
Participant observation is immersion in a culture. Ideally, the ethnographer
lives and works in the community for six months to a year or more ,learning
the language and seeing patterns of behavior over time. Non-participant
observation involves merely watching what is happening and recording
events on the spot.
9. Enlist 5 qualitative research John W Creswell in his book?
Five qualitative research methods are discussed in this subject as
discussed by John W. Creswell in his book. Following are the five qualitative
research methods:
1. Narrative Research. 2. Phenomenology 3. Grounded Theory. 4.
Ethnography. 5. Case Study
10. Explain function of record in focus group?

Keep a record of the content as well as emotional reactions and nature of
group interactions. Record the following:
-Date, time, and place.
-Names and characteristics of participants.
-Description of group dynamics
3 Marks Questions
11. Difference between survey interview and field research interview?

Survey Interview: It has a clear beginning and end. • The same standard
questions are asked and in same sequence.
• Interviewer appears neutral at all times. Interviewer asks questions, and
the respondent answers. • It is almost always with one respondent alone.
Professional tone and business like focus; diversions ignored. • Closed
ended Qs are common; rare probes. • Interviewer controls the pace and
direction of interview. Social context of interview is ignored and assumed to
make no difference. • Interviewer attempts to mold the communication in a
standard framework.
FR Interview: The beginning and end are not clear. • Questions and order
are tailored to specific people and situations. • Interviewer shows interest
in responses, encourages elaboration. It is like a friendly conversational
exchange, with more interviewer questions. • It can occur in group setting
or with others in area. Interspersed with jokes, stories, diversions. • Open
ended Qs are common; probes frequent. • Interviewer and member jointly
control the pace and direction of interview. Social context of interview is
noted and seen as important for interpreting the meaning or responses. •
Interviewer adjusts to member‘s norms and language usage.

12. Enlist 6 features of theoretical framework?
1. Make an inventory of variables
2. Specify the direction of relationship
3. Logic for the proposed relationship
4. Make an inventory of propositions
5. Arrange propositions sequentially
6. Present schematic diagram
13. Enlist parts of main body of report?
Introduction: -- Background -- Objectives Methodology. Results can be
divided into different areas. Limitations. Conclusions and recommendations
References. Acknowledgements.
Appended parts Data collection forms (questionnaires, check list, interview
guide, other forms). Detailed calculations. General tables. Other support
material. Bibliography, if needed.
14. Difference between ethnography and phenomenology?
Phenomenology: A phenomenological study describes the meaning for
several individuals of their lived experiences of a concept or a phenomenon.

The basic purpose of phenomenology is to reduce individual experiences
with a phenomenon to a description of the universal essence.
Ethnography: Ethnography is a qualitative design in which the researcher
describes and interprets the shared and learned patterns of values,

Assignment No. 2

 By Hafiza Expert Zoologist
BT-406 Research Methodology & Skill Enhancement

                                          Total Marks: 5

                                   Due Date: 11-05-2025

    How have historical atrocities, such as Nazi human experiments, shaped
modern ethical standards and regulations in medical research, and what are
the lasting implications of these influences on current research practices?

  •   Established in 1947 in response to Nazi human experiments.
  •   Emphasized voluntary consent as essential.
  •   Required that experiments yield fruitful results for the good of society.
  •   Stressed the necessity to avoid unnecessary physical and mental suffering.

  •   Adopted in 1964 by the World Medical Association.
  •   Built upon the Nuremberg Code, focusing on medical research ethics.
  •   Introduced the requirement for independent ethical review.
  •   Prioritized the well-being of research subjects over scientific interests. (Verywell Health)

  •   Published in 1979 in the United States.
  •   Outlined three core principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.
  •   Provided a framework for ethical research involving human subjects.
  •   Influenced federal regulations and the establishment of Institutional Review Boards (IRBs).

  •   Modern research ethics are grounded in these foundational documents.
  •   Emphasis on informed consent, risk-benefit analysis, and equitable subject selection.
  •   Ongoing revisions and updates ensure relevance to contemporary research challenges.
      (ResearchGate)

    Considering the historical exclusion of women from research studies due to
fetal safety concerns, how should modern biomedical research balance the
ethical challenges of inclusivity, fetal protection, and scientific validity?

  •   Women, especially pregnant women, were often excluded from clinical trials.
  •   Concerns centered around potential risks to fetuses.
  •   Resulted in a lack of data on women's health and treatment responses.

  •   Respect for Persons:
        o Acknowledges the autonomy of all individuals, including women.

        o  Supports informed consent and voluntary participation.
  •   Justice:
        o Advocates for fair distribution of research benefits and burdens.
        o Encourages inclusion of diverse populations to ensure generalizable results.

  •   Implementation of rigorous safety protocols to protect both women and fetuses.
  •   Designing studies that specifically address sex-based differences.
  •   Ensuring transparent communication about potential risks and benefits.

  •   Inclusion of women enhances the scientific validity of research findings.
  •   Ethical frameworks support the protection of vulnerable populations while promoting inclusivity.
  •   Ongoing ethical oversight ensures that studies adapt to emerging concerns and data.

   With the rise of genomic medicine and gene editing technologies, where
should the ethical line be drawn between therapeutic innovation and the
potential resurgence of eugenic ideologies?

  •   Gene editing offers potential cures for genetic diseases.
  •   Therapeutic applications aim to alleviate suffering and improve quality of life.
  •   Ethical guidelines support interventions that have clear medical benefits.

  •   Non-therapeutic enhancements raise concerns about social inequality.
  •   Potential misuse of technology for trait selection reminiscent of eugenics.
  •   Challenges in defining the boundaries between therapy and enhancement.

  •   Declaration of Helsinki:
        o Emphasizes that the well-being of the subject should take precedence over the interests of
           science and society.
        o Requires that medical research is conducted by scientifically qualified individuals and under
           ethical standards. (Wikipedia, Verywell Health)
  •   Belmont Report:
        o Beneficence:
              ▪ Obligation to maximize possible benefits and minimize potential harms.
        o Justice:
              ▪ Ensures equitable access to the benefits of research and protection against exploitation.

  •   Clear distinction between therapeutic and enhancement applications.
  •   Robust regulatory frameworks to oversee gene editing research.
  •   Engagement with diverse stakeholders to guide ethical decision-making.
  •   Continuous ethical review to adapt to technological advancements.

Research Misconduct:
Research Misconduct can be characterised as actions or questionable research practices that
fall short of the standards of ethics, research and scholarship required to ensure that the
integrity of research is upheld.
Forms of research Misconduct:
Fabrication: This refers to the practice of making up data without having done the required
research.
Falsification: This type of research misconduct involves the wilful manipulation of data,
materials, processes, or equipment to arrive at a predefined conclusion.

Plagiarism: This is one of the most common types of research misconduct, and involves using
another person’s ideas, content, writing, processes, or results without giving due credit.
Authorship: This type of ethical misconduct in research includes attempts to assign false
authorships without adequate contribution to research, mentioning authors without their
consent, or failing to include authors who are original contributors.
Conflicts of interest: This can be classified under general research misconduct and involves
lapses by researchers in declaring any conflict of interests in their research work.
Approvals: One of the most important aspect of research that involves human or animal
subjects is adhering to all the ethical approvals and legal guidelines.

      Introduction

      The rapid advancements in technology and the exponential growth of data analytics have
      profoundly transformed research methodologies across various disciplines. These changes have
      not only enhanced the capabilities of researchers but have also introduced new challenges and
      considerations regarding the reliability, validity, and ethical implications of research. This essay
      will explore the key ways in which technology and data analytics have reshaped research
      methodologies, and the corresponding implications for the research process.

      The Rise of Big Data and Data-Driven Research

      Subheading: The Emergence of Big Data

      The proliferation of digital technologies, the ubiquity of internet-connected devices, and the
      increasing digitization of information have led to the exponential growth of data, commonly
      referred to as "Big Data." This vast and diverse collection of structured and unstructured data has
      revolutionized the way researchers approach and conduct their investigations.

      Subheading: Data-Driven Research Methodologies

The availability of large, complex datasets has given rise to data-driven research methodologies,
where researchers leverage advanced analytical tools and techniques to uncover patterns, trends,
and insights that were previously inaccessible. This shift has enabled researchers to move beyond
traditional hypothesis-driven approaches and explore data in a more exploratory and inductive
manner.

Subheading: Advantages of Data-Driven Research

The adoption of data-driven research methodologies has brought about several advantages,
including:

1. Increased Scope and Scale: Researchers can now access and analyze larger, more
comprehensive datasets, allowing for more robust and generalizable findings.

2. Enhanced Precision and Granularity: The ability to process and analyze vast amounts of data
has enabled researchers to uncover more nuanced and granular insights.

3. Faster Insights and Iterative Processes: The speed and efficiency of data analysis have
accelerated the research process, allowing for more iterative and responsive approaches.

4. Interdisciplinary Collaboration: The interdisciplinary nature of data-driven research has
fostered collaboration across various fields, leading to more holistic and multifaceted
understandings of complex phenomena.

The Democratization of Research Tools and Techniques

Subheading: Accessible and User-Friendly Research Tools

Advancements in technology have led to the development of a wide range of user-friendly research
tools and software that are more accessible to researchers across disciplines. These tools, such as
data visualization software, statistical analysis packages, and online survey platforms, have
lowered the barriers to entry for conducting research, enabling even those with limited technical
expertise to engage in sophisticated data analysis and visualization.

Subheading: Citizen Science and Crowdsourcing

The democratization of research tools has also facilitated the rise of citizen science and
crowdsourcing initiatives, where members of the public can actively participate in the research
process. These approaches have expanded the reach and scale of research projects, tapping into
the collective knowledge and resources of diverse communities.

Subheading: Implications for Collaboration and Interdisciplinarity

The increased accessibility of research tools has fostered greater collaboration and
interdisciplinary work. Researchers from different backgrounds can now more easily share data,
exchange ideas, and work together on complex, multifaceted research projects, leading to more
comprehensive and innovative solutions.

       The Shift Towards Computational and Simulation-Based Research

Subheading: Computational Modeling and Simulation

Advancements in computing power and the availability of sophisticated software have enabled
researchers to develop and utilize computational models and simulations to study complex
phenomena. These approaches allow researchers to explore scenarios, test hypotheses, and make
predictions in silico, without the need for extensive physical experimentation or data collection.

Subheading: Advantages of Computational and Simulation-Based Research

Computational and simulation-based research methodologies offer several advantages, including:

1. Reduced Time and Cost: Simulations can be conducted more efficiently and cost-effectively
compared to traditional experimental approaches.

2. Increased Flexibility and Scalability: Computational models can be easily modified and scaled
to explore a wider range of scenarios and variables.

3. Enhanced Precision and Control: Simulations provide researchers with greater control over
experimental conditions and the ability to isolate specific factors.

4. Ethical Considerations: Computational and simulation-based approaches can address ethical
concerns by reducing the need for experiments involving human or animal subjects.

Subheading: Limitations and Challenges

While computational and simulation-based research methodologies offer significant benefits, they
also come with their own set of limitations and challenges, such as the need for robust validation,
the potential for oversimplification, and the reliance on the quality and accuracy of the underlying
models and data.

 What the researcher trying to accomplish.

Goals of Exploratory Research:
  Become familiar with the topic. Develop well grounded
   picture of the situation.

  Formulate questions and refine issues for more
   systematic inquiry.

  b. Descriptive Research:

    Research designed to describe characteristics of the

  profile of a group.

 Create a set of categories or classify.

  Provide evidence to support or refute an explanation or
   prediction.

1. Explain the different approaches to conducting a literature review. (2
marks)

The article identifies three main approaches to conducting a literature review:

   1. Systematic Literature Review:
      A rigorous and structured method developed primarily in medical science. It involves a
      predefined search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and aims to synthesize all
      relevant empirical studies to answer a specific research question.
   2. Semi-Systematic (Narrative) Review:
      Used when a topic is broad, interdisciplinary, or has been conceptualized differently
      across fields. It maps themes, theoretical developments, and identifies research gaps
      without necessarily including every study.
   3. Integrative Review:
      This approach critiques and synthesizes literature to develop new theories or conceptual
      models. It combines insights from diverse sources and is often applied to mature or
      emerging topics.

2. Explain the purpose of different approaches to conducting a literature
review. (2 marks)

   •   Systematic Review Purpose:
       To gather and evaluate all empirical evidence on a narrowly defined research question,
       often to inform policy or practice by showing evidence of effect.
   •   Semi-Systematic Review Purpose:
       To provide an overview of a topic across different disciplines, identify patterns and
       knowledge gaps, and track research development over time.

Q1. How have historical atrocities, such as Nazi human experiments, shaped
modern ethical standards and regulations in medical research, and what are the
lasting implications of these influences on current research practices?

Historical atrocities—particularly the Nazi human experiments during the Third Reich—
profoundly shaped the ethical landscape of modern biomedical research. As documented by Artal
and Rubenfeld (2017), Nazi physicians conducted coercive, lethal experiments on prisoners,
including Jews, Roma, and the disabled, with no informed consent and often with fatal outcomes
(p. 3). These included forced sterilizations, hypothermia studies, and pathogenic exposure among
others, all under the justification of racial cleansing and eugenics-driven ideology.

The global revulsion to these atrocities led directly to the Nuremberg Code (1947), which
established voluntary consent, risk minimization, and the right to withdraw as fundamental
principles of human subject research. This was followed by the Declaration of Helsinki (1964)
and the Belmont Report (1979), which codified ethical principles such as autonomy, beneficence,
non-maleficence, and justice (Artal & Rubenfeld, 2017, pp. 4–5).

These foundational documents continue to shape modern Institutional Review Boards (IRBs)
and research protocols. The legacy of Nazi crimes remains a persistent reminder of the need for

  Inbox for paid LMs Work & Project Handing at M.Kashif(03064963933)

strict oversight, transparency, and ethical vigilance in research. The global ethical frameworks
today—such as the Common Rule in the U.S.—are direct safeguards ensuring that such abuses
are never repeated.

Q2. Considering the historical exclusion of women from research studies due to
fetal safety concerns, how should modern biomedical research balance the ethical
challenges of inclusivity, fetal protection, and scientific validity?

Historically, women—especially pregnant women—were excluded from clinical research due
to fears over harming a potential fetus. This exclusion, while protective in intent, resulted in a
critical lack of data on how medications and interventions affect women differently (Artal &
Rubenfeld, 2017, p. 6).

The authors highlight the evolving concept of the fetus as a patient, which introduces ethical
tensions: How do we ensure scientific validity through gender-inclusive trials, while upholding
fetal protection? The current approach, grounded in respect for autonomy and beneficence,
supports the inclusion of women in research while ensuring proper risk disclosure through
informed consent (p. 6).

Modern research must balance:

   •   Justice: Fair inclusion of women to prevent gender-biased data;
   •   Autonomy: Women's right to choose participation even in pregnancy;
   •   Scientific validity: Ensuring that findings are generalizable to all populations;
   •   Non-maleficence: Avoiding harm to both the mother and fetus.

Thus, the ethical challenge lies in designing studies with robust monitoring, risk-benefit analysis,
and alternative study models (e.g., observational studies or post-marketing surveillance), while
integrating women in a responsible and scientifically meaningful way.

Q3. With the rise of genomic medicine and gene editing technologies, where should
the ethical line be drawn between therapeutic innovation and the potential
resurgence of eugenic ideologies?

Artal and Rubenfeld (2017) express concern that emerging tools like CRISPR-Cas9 blur the line
between therapy and eugenics. While gene editing holds promise for treating inherited diseases,
it also presents a pathway for non-therapeutic enhancements—potentially reviving the eugenics
logic that fueled historical atrocities (pp. 7–8).

The authors warn that gene-editing could enable "designer babies", social discrimination, and
violations of medical privacy. This concern is compounded by real-world precedents—such as
Chinese researchers editing embryonic genes and creating genetically modified monkeys (p. 7).
  Inbox for paid LMs Work & Project Handing at M.Kashif(03064963933)

To prevent misuse, ethical lines must be drawn:

   •   Therapeutic use only: Editing for disease prevention or treatment should be distinct from
       enhancement purposes.
   •   Public policy: Strict regulation by independent bioethics committees and government
       oversight is essential.
   •   Equity and access: Preventing genetic “elitism” through fair access to innovations.
   •   International consensus: Establishing global norms, as research often transcends national
       boundaries.

The researcher focuses on an issue or concern, and then selects one bounded case

 Focus is on the case itself because the case presents an unusual or unique
situation.

notions so that the analytic, substantive theory can emerge.

or when the theory is sufficiently detailed.
3- The researcher needs to recognize that the primary outcome of this study is a
theory with specific components: a central phenomenon, causal conditions,
strategies, conditions and context, and consequences.

5-Explain Discriminant Validity (5)
Also called divergent validity, discriminant validity is the opposite of convergent
validity.
It means that the indicators of one construct hang together or converge, but also
diverge or are negatively associated with opposing constructs.
It says that if two constructs A and B are very different, then measures of
A and B should not be associated.
For example, we have 10 items that measure political conservatism.
People answer all 10 in similar ways.
But we have also put 5 questions in the same questionnaire that measure political
liberalism.
Our measure of conservatism has discriminant validity if the 10 conservatism items
hang together and are negatively associated with 5 liberalism ones.

Question 1
What is the type of case studies
Answer
Single Instrumental Case Study: The researcher focuses on a specific issue and studies one example to explain it.
Collective/Multiple Case Study: The researcher focuses on the same issue but looks at multiple examples to explain it better.
Intrinsic Case Study: The researcher focuses on one unique or unusual case because it’s interesting on its own.
Question 2
Challenges in case studies
Answer
    1. The researcher must decided which bounded system to study.

Difference between cross sectional study and longitudinal study
Answer
    1. Cross-Sectional Study:
Data is collected at one point in time.
It shows how things are at that moment (like a snapshot).
Example: Surveying people’s health in 2025.
Good for: Finding out how common something is, or comparing different groups.
Limitations: Can’t show changes over time or cause-and-effect.
    2. Longitudinal Study:
Data is collected over a long period.
It tracks how things change over time.
Example: Following people’s health from childhood to adulthood.
Good for: Understanding changes and causes over time.
Limitations: Takes time and is more expensive.

 difference between index and scale

What are participants observation?
Answer
In participant observation, researchers can be:
    1. Complete participants – They join the group and act like regular members, without telling anyone they are studying them.
    2. Covert participants – They secretly observe the group without revealing they are a researcher.
    3. Overt participants – They openly tell the group they are a researcher while still taking part in the activities.
Question 10
Quantitative research
Answer
Quantitative research is a way of studying things by collecting numbers and data that can be measured. It helps researchers find patterns or trends using math and statistics.
 For example, surveys or experiments are often used to collect this data. The aim is to understand things in a clear, number-based way that can help make predictions or draw conclusions.
Question 11
Exploratory and co-relational hypothesis
Answer
Exploratory Hypothesis: Used when exploring a new topic to find patterns or ideas, without predicting specific outcomes.
Correlational Hypothesis: Suggests a connection between two things (like more study time and better grades) but doesn’t say one causes the other.
Question 12
Semi-structured and unstructured interview
Answer
Semi-structured Interview: Has some planned questions but allows flexibility to ask more based on answers.
Unstructured Interview: No fixed questions, just a free-flowing conversation.
Question 13
Ethical  research
Answer
Ethical research means doing studies in a fair and honest way. Key ideas are:
    1. Informed Consent: People know what the study is about and agree to join.
    2. Confidentiality: Personal details stay private.
    3. Minimizing Harm: Researchers try not to cause any harm or discomfort.
    4. Honesty: Results are reported truthfully.
    5. Fairness: Everyone is treated equally.
    6. Respect: People can leave the study anytime if they want.
Question 14
Difference between qualitative and quantitative research
Answer
    1. Data Type:
Qualitative: Uses words or descriptions.
Quantitative: Uses numbers and stats.
    2. Goal:
Qualitative: Understands feelings, experiences, and ideas.
Quantitative: Measures and counts things to find patterns.
    3. Methods:
Qualitative: Interviews, observations, and open-ended questions.
Quantitative: Surveys, tests, and structured questions.
    4. Analysis:
Qualitative: Looks for themes or meanings.
Quantitative: Uses math and statistics to analyze data.
    5. Outcome:
Qualitative: Provides in-depth understanding.
Quantitative: Gives clear, measurable results.
Question 15
FGD limitations
Here are the limitations of FGDs in simple terms:
    1. Dominant Voices: Some people may take over the discussion.
    2. Small Group: It might not represent everyone.
    3. Bias: The facilitator or group may influence responses.
    4. Time-Consuming: It takes a lot of time to organize and analyze.
    5. Shallow Answers: Doesn’t provide deep individual insights.
Question 16
Sequential sampling
Answer
Sequential sampling is when you collect data one step at a time and make decisions as you go. You don’t wait until you have all the data; instead, you stop or continue based on what you find along the way. It helps save time and effort. This method is used in things like checking product quality or testing new ideas.
Question 17
Steps for conducting an experiment
Answer
Here are the simple steps for conducting an experiment:

    1. Ask a question: What do you want to learn?
    2. Research: Find out what’s already known about the topic.
    3. Make a guess: Predict what will happen (hypothesis).
    4. Plan: Decide how to test your guess.

A theoretical framework is conceptual model of how one theorizes or makes logical sense of the
relationships among several factors that have been identified as important to the problem under
study. These factors which may also be called as variables may have been identified through
such processes as interviews with informants, observations, and literature survey. The theoretical
framework discusses the interrelationships among the variables that are considered to be integral
to the dynamics of the situation being investigated..

      The Components of the Theoretical Framework
      A good theoretical framework identifies and labels the important variables in
      the situation that are relevant to the problem identified. It logically describes
      the interconnections among these variables.
       The relationships among the independent variables, the dependent variable(s),
       and if applicable, the moderating and intervening variables are elaborated.

       The elaboration of the variables in the theoretical framework addresses the
       issues of why or how we expect certain relationships to exist, and the nature
       and direction of the relationships among the variables of interest. At the end,
       the whole discussion can be portrayed in a schematic diagram. There are six
       basic features that should be incorporated in any theoretical framework. These
       features are:

1. Make an inventory of variables: For developing a framework it
   appears essential to identify the factors relevant to the problem under
   study. These factors are the empirical realities which can be named at
   some abstract level called concepts. The concepts taking more than one
   value are the variables. In other words, the researcher makes an
   inventory of relevant variables. The variables considered relevant to
   the study should be clearly identified and labeled in the discussion.

2. Specify the direction of relationship: If the nature and direction of
   relationship can be theorized on the basis of the findings of previous
   research, then there should be an indication in the discussion as to
   whether the relationship should be positive or negative.

   relationships to exist. There should be clear explanation of why we
   would expect these relationships to exist. The arguments could be

   how two or more variables are related to one another. This should be

   different variables.

Scale is a measure to capture the intensity, direction, level, or potency of a variable. Arranges responses on a
continuum. A scale can use single indicator or multiple indicators. Ordinal level.

Index is a measure in which researcher adds or combines several distinct indicators of a construct into a single
score. Composite score.

The two popular approaches to grounded theory are the systematic procedures of Strauss and Corbin (1990, 1998) and the constructivist approach of Charmaz (2005, 2006). In the more systematic, the investigator seeks to systematically develop a theory that explains process, action, or interaction on a topic. The researcher typically conducts 20 to 30 interviews based on several visits "to the field" to collect interview data to saturate the categories (or find information that continues to add to them until no more can be found). A category represents a unit of information composed of events, happenings, and instances (Strauss & Corbin, 1990).

Enlist 6 features of theoretical framework 3
A theoretical framework is conceptual model of how one theorizes or makes logical sense of the relationships among several factors that have been identified as important to the problem under study. These factors which may also be called as variables may have been identified through such processes as interviews with informants, observations, and literature survey. The theoretical framework discusses the interrelationships among the variables that are considered to be integral to the dynamics of the situation being investigated..
The Components of the Theoretical Framework

A good theoretical framework identifies and labels the important variables in the situation that are relevant to the problem identified. It logically describes the interconnections among these variables.

The relationships among the independent variables, the dependent variable(s), and if applicable, the moderating and intervening variables are elaborated.

The elaboration of the variables in the theoretical framework addresses the issues of why or how we expect certain relationships to exist, and the nature and direction of the relationships among the variables of interest. At the end, the whole discussion can be portrayed in a schematic diagram. There are six basic features that should be incorporated in any theoretical framework. These features are:

    1. Make an inventory of variables: For developing a framework it appears essential to identify the factors relevant to the problem under study. These factors are the empirical realities which can be named at some abstract level called concepts. The concepts taking more than one value are the variables. In other words, the researcher makes an inventory of relevant variables. The variables considered relevant to the study should be clearly identified and labeled in the discussion.

    2. Specify the direction of relationship: If the nature and direction of relationship can be theorized on the basis of the findings of previous research, then there should be an indication in the discussion as to whether the relationship should be positive or negative.

    3. Give a clear explanation of why we should expect the proposed relationships to exist. There should be clear explanation of why we would expect these relationships to exist. The arguments could be drawn from the previous research findings. The discussions should state how two or more variables are related to one another. This should be done for the important relationships that are theorized to exist among the variables. It is essential to theorize logical relationship between different variables.

    4. Make an inventory of propositions: Stipulation of logical relationship between any two variables means the formulation of a proposition. If such relationships have been proposed between different variables, it will result in the formulation of a number of propositions. Let us call such a collection of propositions as an inventory of propositions. Each proposition is backed up by strong theoretical argumentation.

    5. Arrange these propositions in a sequential order: one proposition generates the next proposition, which generates the next following proposition, which in turn generates the next following proposition, and so on. This is an axiomatic way of the derivation of propositions. Resultantly it will provide us a sequentially arranged set of propositions which are interlinked and interlocked with each other. Theory, if you remember, is an interrelated set of propositions. Therefore, the present interrelated set of propositions relevant to a particular problem is in fact a theoretical framework explaining the pathways of logical relationships between different variables.

     Whether we are aware of it or not, we are surrounded by research. Educators, administrators, government
     officials, business leaders, human service providers, health care professionals, regularly use social research
     findings in their jobs. Social research can be used to raise children, reduce crime, improve public health, sell
     products, improve workers’ efficiency, or just understand one’s life.
     Assume for the moment that you are the Manager of a restaurant. You are experiencing a significant turnover
     in your waiter/waitress pool, and long-time customers have been commenting that thefriendly atmosphere that
     has historically drawn them to your door is changing. What will you do? Where will you try to solve this
     problem? The problem of high turnover and decline in the friendly atmosphere at the restaurant has to be
     researched.
     The study of research methods provides you with the knowledge and skills you need to solve the problem and
     meet the challenges of a fast-paced decision-making environment. A systematic inquiry whose objective is to
     provide information to the problems (be they managerial as in our example) is one way to explain research.
     What is Research?
     General image of the research is that it has something to do with the laboratory where scientists are supposedly
     doing some experiments. Somebody who is interviewing consumers to find out their opinion about the new
     packaging of milk is also doing research. Research is simply the process of finding solutions to a problem after
     through study and analysis of the situational factors. It is gathering information needed to answer a question,
     and thereby help in solving a problem. We do not do study in any haphazard manner. Instead we try to follow a
     system or a procedure in an organized manner. It is all the more necessary in case we want to repeat the study,
     or somebody else wants to verify our findings. In the latter case the other person has to follow the same
     procedure that we followed. Hence not only we have to do the study in a systematic manner but also that system
     should be known to others.
     What is the value of Research?
     The nature of research problems could vary. Problems may refer to some undesirable situation or these may
     refer to simply a curiosity of the researcher that may be agitating his or her mind. For example, in a recent
     BA/BS examination of the Punjab University 67 percent of the students failed. That is a colossal wastage of the
     resources, hence an undesirable situation that needs research to find a solution. The researcher may come up
     with a variety of reasons that may relate with the students, the teachers, the curricula, the availability of books,
     the examination system, the family environment of the student, and many more. So, a study may be carried out
     diagnose the situation, and the recommendations to be applied to overcome the undesirable situation of mass
     failure of students.
     In the same examination result one finds that girls have captured a good number of top positions; and that is
     happening for the last couple of years. One gets curious and tries to do research for finding out the reasons.
     This is an academic problem but certainly a research problem. Conducting such research offers the pleasure
     of solving a puzzle. Why the girls are catching most of the top positions in different examination? This might
     be a puzzle that the research may like to explain. Such findings make a good contribution to the body of
     knowledge i.e. making some good discoveries as part of the basic research. Finding answer to any enigma is
     self-satisfying.
     The researchers try to make use of their findings for generating theories and models that could be used for
     understanding human behavior and the functioning of different structures both at the micro (organizational)
     and macro (societal) level.
     Therefore, research may be considered as an organized, systematic, data based, critical, objective, scientific
     inquiry or investigation into a specific problem, undertaken with the purpose of finding answers or solutions to
     it. In this way research provides the needed information that guides the planners to make informed decisions to
     successfully deal with the problems. The information provided could be the result of a careful analysis of data
     gathered firsthand or of the data that are already available with an organization.
     The value of research for policy makers, planners, business managers, and other stakeholders is that it reduces
     uncertainty by providing information that improves the decision-making process. The decision- making process

2.   Diagnosing and assessing problems or opportunities;
3.   Selecting and implementing a course of action; and

MUHAMMAD IMRAN BT406 Research Methodology & Skill
                                                Enhancement
 Past papers solved questions                                                              MID TERM
1. Parties in research?
Mostly three parties:
  1. The researcher
  2. The sponsoring client (user)
  3. The respondent (subject)
2. Role of theory in science? Role of theory in Research?
Theory as orientation. Framework. Phenomenon may be studied in different ways. Narrows the range of facts
to be studied. Study of football.
    • Theory as conceptualization and classification. Provides concepts.
    • Theory in summarizing role. Empirical generalizations.
    • Theory predicts facts. Extrapolation.
    • Theory points gaps in knowledge.
3. Theoretical framework and its basic point?
A good theoretical framework identifies and labels the important variables in the situation that are relevant to
the problem identified. It logically describes the interconnections among these variables

   1.   Make an inventory of variables
   2.   Specify the direction of relationship
   3.   Give a clear explanation of why we should expect the proposed relationships to exist.
   4.   Make an inventory of propositions
   5.   Arrange these propositions in a sequential order 6. Schematic diagram of the theoretical model be given.

4. Three responsibility of participant?
  No physical harm, discomfort, pain, embarrassment, or loss of privacy. Follow three guidelines:
1. Explain study benefits.
2. Explain respondent rights and protections.
3. Obtain informed consent.

5. Two basic power of research? Two basic power of knowledge?
Empiricism:
  • Sensory experience
  • positivism.
Rationalism:
  • Explanation for regularity.
  • Consequential arguments.
  • Logical.

6. Source of concept?
We create concepts from personal experience. Mass, speed, family. we borrow from other disciplines. We
develop a specialized jargon or terminology for a Particular subject

7. Purposive sampling?
Researcher lays down the criteria for the subjects. Also called as judgmental or expert opinion sample.
Selection depends upon the judgment of selector

8. Theoretical review?
Compare how different theories address an issue. Evaluate different theories for the soundness of their
assumptions, logical consistency, and scope of explanation. Researcher may integrate two theories – form a
hybrid

9. Relationship of variable?

                                                                                      MUHAMMAD IMRAN           1

Relationship among variables. Logical. A statement concerned with the theoretical relationship among
variables is a proposition. If the relationship refers to an observable reality, then the proposition may be
testable call it a hypothesis

10.    Name the parties in research?
Mostly three parties:
    • The researcher
    • The sponsoring client (user)
    • The respondent (subject)
Interaction requires ethical questions.
 Each party expects certain rights and feels certain obligations.

11.    Exploratory and descriptive research?
Exploratory: Initial research conducted to clarify and define the nature of the problem. Exploring a new topic.
  Specifically, there could be number of goals of exploratory research.
Ddescriptive: Research designed to describe characteristics of the phenomenon understudy. Helps in
diagnostic analysis

12.    Dependent and independent variable?
An independent variable is the variable that is changed or controlled in a scientific experiment to test the
effects on the dependent variable. A dependent variable is the variable being tested and measured in a
scientific experiment. The dependent variable is 'dependent' on the independent variable.

13.    Right of participant?
  No physical harm, discomfort, pain, embarrassment, or loss of privacy. Follow three guidelines: 1. Explain
study benefits. 2. Explain respondent rights and protections. 3. Obtain informed consent.

14.    Validation of experiment?
Validity refers to confidence in cause and effect relationship.     Internal validity is high in Laboratory
experiments. External validity (generalizability) is not sure.

15.    Several way to protect confidentiality in research? 5
  Obtaining signed nondisclosure documents. Restricting access to respondent‘s identification Revealing
respondent information only with written consent. Restricting access to data instruments where the
respondent is identified. Nondisclosure of data subsets.

16.    External validity in research? 5
External validity (generalizability) is not sure. Organizational or field setting. Several confounding variables.
Field experiments have more external validity but less internal validity. • First have lab experiments then test in
field setting.

17.    Cross sectional and longitudinal studies? 5
Cross-Sectional Research: Observe at one point in time, Snapshot study
Longitudinal Research: Examine at more than one time. Can be • Time series study. • Panel study. •
Cohort study – Category of people who share the same experience.

18.    How to locate research report? 5
  Articles in scholarly journals. Locating the relevant articles is difficult. Many academic field have
―abstracts‖ or ―indexes‖ for scholarly literature. Look in reference section of library Also available on
computer.

19.    Applied criteria of sampling design? 5
   Selecting some of the elements in the population and draw conclusions about the total population.
Population element is the subject on which measurement is being taken. Has its advantages and
disadvantages. Selection of appropriate sampling design

20.    Communication analysis in research? 5
analysis is a systematic, quantitative approach to analyzing the content or meaning of communicative
messages. Content analysis is a descriptive approach to communication research, and as such is used to
describe communicative phenomenon

BT406 Research Methodology &
Skill Enhancement
MSC ZOOLOGY
 MUHAMMAD IMRAN

          MUHAMMAD IMRAN

 1. Introduction to Research
 Objectives of the Course
 Students should be able to:
    • Sharpen the analytical skills.
    • Develop their understanding of the research concerns.
    • Develop the ability to convert the research concerns into a research problem.
    • Prepare a roadmap or blueprint of the research – using appropriate methodologies.
 Conduct the research by following the complete research process.
 Methodology
 Grading
   Textbook:
  Neuman, W. L. (2000).

   Social Research Methods: Qualitative and Quantitative Approaches. Boston: Allyen and Bacon.
 Supplementary books:
  Zikmund, W. G. (2003). Business Research Methods. Mason, Ohio: South Western.

  Sekaran, U. (2004). Research Methods for Business New York: John Wiley & Sons.

 What is research?
  Gathering information needed to answer a question, and thereby help in solving a problem.

  Systematic and organized effort to investigate.

   What is the value of research?
 Research offers the pleasure of solving a puzzle.
   Generating Theories – Models
 Identifying problems and solutions
    Research helps to develop new methodologies
     We are surrounded by social research

 2. Scientific Methods of Research

 RESEARCH METHODS SCIENTIFIC METHODS OF RESEARCH Every human knowledge is not
 science
 Science is a method
 A procedure to produce knowledge i.e. discovering uniformities/ principle” es, laws in this universe.
 Process of “sensory experiences
• Observation

 •      Repetition
  •     Reobservation.
• By repeating the observation researchers want to be definite/positive.

 This approach is called positivism
 Results are organized, systematized, and made part of the body of knowledge.
  Special Features of Scientific Method
    1. Empirical
 Observable phenomenon
    2. Verifiable
 • Use senses to confirm or refute    the observation.
 • “Sensory experiences”
 • Intuitions and revelations are out.
 • Replicability needed.

 3. Cumulative

                                                                              MUHAMMAD IMRAN        1

  •       Knowledge grows.
  •       Need not start from scratch.
4. Deterministic
  •     Explains why things happen?
  •     Parsimony
           Minimum No. of variables that explain variance.
 5. Ethical and ideological neutrality
 Value free.
 Objectivity.
  Is it possible?
      6. Statistical generalization
      7. Rationalism
 Employ rigorous rules of logic.
 Argumentation.

All features are interrelated.
Scientists not necessarily adhere to all these characteristics.
Two power bases of knowledge
 Empiricism: Sensory experience
                     positivism.
 Rationalism: Explanation for regularity. Consequential arguments. Logical.
Any body following the said procedure of research is doing scientific research.
Logical positivism i.e. theory + observation + statistics

3. Classification of Research
          Four main dimensions:
      1. Purpose of doing research.
      2. Intended uses of research.
      3. How it treats time → time dimension.
      4. The research techniques used
Purpose of Research:
What the researcher trying to accomplish.
      1. Exploratory/ Formulative
      2. Descriptive
      3. Explanatory
      4. Studies can be multi-purpose
a. Exploratory Research:
      ▪     Initial research conducted to clarify and define the nature of the problem. Exploring a new
          topic.
      ▪   Specifically, there could be number of goals of exploratory research.
Goals of Exploratory Research:
      ▪   Become familiar with the topic. Develop well grounded picture of the situation.
      ▪   Develop tentative theories.
      ▪   Determine the feasibility of study.
      ▪   Formulate questions and refine issues for more systematic inquiry.
                                                                                  MUHAMMAD IMRAN     2

   ▪   Develop techniques and a sense of direction for future research
b. Descriptive Research:
    Research designed to describe characteristics of the phenomenon understudy.
    Helps in diagnostic analysis
Goals of Descriptive Research:
   ▪   Describe the situation/characteristics. Provide an accurate profile of a group.
   ▪   Give a verbal or numerical picture (%).
   ▪   Present basic background information.
   ▪   Create a set of categories or classify.
   ▪   Clarify sequence, set of stages.
   ▪   Focus on ‘who’, ‘what’, ‘when’, ‘where’ and ‘how’ but not on ‘why’.
c. Explanatory Research:
   ▪   Also called as causal research i.e.
   ▪   ‘Why’? Explanation.
   ▪   Identify cause and effect relationship among different factors.
Goals of Explanatory Research:
   ▪   Explain things not just reporting. Why?
   ▪   Which explanation is better.
   ▪   Determine the accuracy of theory.
   ▪   Advance knowledge about underlying process
   ▪   Build and elaborate a theory → complete.
   ▪   Extend a theory or principle into new areas.
   ▪   Provide evidence to support or refute an explanation or prediction.
2. Intended Uses of Research:
   a. Basic Research
   ▪   Pure/ fundamental/ academic
   ▪   Developing/ refuting/ supporting theories.
   ▪   Expand knowledge.
   ▪   Explanatory research is the most common
   ▪   Applied can also contribute.
b. Applied Research:
   ▪   Solve specific problems → help practitioners. Market new product.
   ▪   Choose one policy over the other.
   ▪   For improving productivity → problem with machines, raw material, persons working.

Basic and Applied Research Comparison
Basic Research
   ▪   Intrinsically satisfying
   ▪   Freedom.
                                                                             MUHAMMAD IMRAN   3

   ▪   High standards applied.
   ▪   Logic and rigorous research design
   ▪   Basic knowledge.
   ▪   Success→ results published, impact on other scientists.

Correct option: c) Code of ethics

8. One of the characteristics of a good hypothesis is that it should be ________.
Options:
a) Practical
b) Based on facts
c) Conceptually clear
d) All of the above
Correct option: c) Conceptually clear

concept.
Options:
a) Behavioral dimensions
b) Facets
c) Properties
d) All of the above
Correct option: d) All of the above

10. The validity of an indicator is verified by comparing it with another measure of
the same construct in which ________.
Options:
a) Published data is available

b) Too much research has been conducted
c) Research is at its early stages
Correct option: a) Published data is available

Lesson 1. INTRODUCTION, DEFINITION & VALUE OF RESEARCH

Whether we are aware of it or not, we are surrounded by research. Educators, administrators,
government officials, business leaders, human service providers, health care professionals, regularly
use social research findings in their jobs. Social research can be used to raise children, reduce crime,
improve public health, sell products, improve workers’ efficiency, or just understand one’s life.

Assume for the moment that you are the Manager of a restaurant. You are experiencing a significant
turnover in your waiter/waitress pool, and long-time customers have been commenting that the friendly
atmosphere that has historically drawn them to your door is changing. What will you do? Where will you
try to solve this problem? The problem of high turnover and decline in the friendly atmosphere at the
restaurant has to be researched.

The study of research methods provides you with the knowledge and skills you need to solve the
problem and meet the challenges of a fast-paced decision-making environment. A systematic inquiry
whose objective is to provide information to the problems (be they managerial as in our example) is one
way to explain research.

What is Research?

General image of the research is that it has something to do with the laboratory where scientists are
supposedly doing some experiments. Somebody who is interviewing consumers to find out their opinion
about the new packaging of milk is also doing research. Research is simply the process of finding
solutions to a problem after through study and analysis of the situational factors. It is gathering
information needed to answer a question, and thereby help in solving a problem. We do not do study in
any haphazard manner. Instead we try to follow a system or a procedure in an organized manner. It is
all the more necessary in case we want to repeat the study, or somebody else wants to verify our
findings. In the latter case the other person has to follow the same procedure that we followed. Hence
not only we have to do the study in a systematic manner but also that system should be known to others.

What is the value of Research?

The nature of research problems could vary. Problems may refer to some undesirable situation or these
may refer to simply a curiosity of the researcher that may be agitating his or her mind. For example, in
a recent BA/BS examination of the Punjab University 67 percent of the students failed. That is a colossal
wastage of the resources, hence an undesirable situation that needs research to find a solution. The
researcher may come up with a variety of reasons that may relate with the students, the teachers, the
curricula, the availability of books, the examination system, the family environment of the student, and
many more. So, a study may be carried out diagnose the situation, and the recommendations to be
applied to overcome the undesirable situation of mass failure of students.

In the same examination result one finds that girls have captured a good number of top positions; and
that is happening for the last couple of years. One gets curious and tries to do research for finding out
the reasons. This is an academic problem but certainly a research problem. Conducting such research
offers the pleasure of solving a puzzle. Why the girls are catching most of the top positions in different
examination? This might be a puzzle that the research may like to explain. Such findings make a good
contribution to the body of knowledge i.e. making some good discoveries as part of the basic research.
Finding answer to any enigma is self-satisfying.
The researchers try to make use of their findings for generating theories and models that could be
used for understanding human behavior and the functioning of different structures both at the micro
(organizational) and macro (societal) level.

Therefore, research may be considered as an organized, systematic, data based, critical, objective, scientific
inquiry or investigation into a specific problem, undertaken with the purpose of finding answers or solutions to
it. In this way research provides the needed information that guides the planners to make informed decisions
to successfully deal with the problems. The information provided could be the result of a careful analysis of
data gathered firsthand or of the data that are already available with an organization.

The value of research for policy makers, planners, business managers, and other stakeholders is that it reduces
uncertainty by providing information that improves the decision-making process. The decision- making process
associated with the development and implementation of a strategy involves four interrelated stages:

   1. Identifying problems or opportunities;
   2. Diagnosing and assessing problems or opportunities;
   3. Selecting and implementing a course of action; and
   4. Evaluating the course of action.

 Identifying problems and solutions to the same problems is in fact applying the research findings to
 overcome an undesirable situation. Initially a problem may appear to be simply a ‘tip of the iceberg’ but the
 study by a professional might help locating the magnitude of the issue as well as its solutions. Such research
 is usually referred to as applied research, which shall be discussed in detail in the coming lectures.

Research helps in developing methodologies

 By now we know that the researchers have to develop methodologies for carrying out the research. These
 methodologies are for the collection of data, data processing and data analysis. For the new researchers, these
 methodologies are already available, most of the researchers just use these. Nevertheless, there is always a
 scope for improvement and certainly new methodologies are developed. Also, we try to borrow methodologies
 from sister subjects.

Lesson 1 INTRODUCTION, DEFINITION & VALUE OF RESEARCH

 Whether we are aware of it or not, we are surrounded by research. Educators, administrators,
 government officials, business leaders, human service providers, health care professionals,
 regularly use social research findings in their jobs. Social research can be used to raise
 children, reduce crime, improve public health, sell products, improve workers’ efficiency, or
 just understand one’s life.

 Assume for the moment that you are the Manager of a restaurant. You are experiencing a
 significant turnover in your waiter/waitress pool, and long-time customers have been
 commenting that the friendly atmosphere that has historically drawn them to your door is
 changing. What will you do? Where will you try to solve this problem? The problem of high
 turnover and decline in the friendly atmosphere at the restaurant has to be researched.

 The study of research methods provides you with the knowledge and skills you need to solve
 the problem and meet the challenges of a fast-paced decision-making environment. A
 systematic inquiry whose objective is to provide information to the problems (be they
 managerial as in our example) is one way to explain research.

 What is Research?

 General image of the research is that it has something to do with the laboratory where
 scientists are supposedly doing some experiments. Somebody who is interviewing
 consumers to find out their opinion about the new packaging of milk is also doing research.
 Research is simply the process of finding solutions to a problem after through study and
 analysis of the situational factors. It is gathering information needed to answer a question,
 and thereby help in solving a problem. We do not do study in any haphazard manner. Instead
 we try to follow a system or a procedure in an organized manner. It is all the more necessary
 in case we want to repeat the study, or somebody else wants to verify our findings. In the
 latter case the other person has to follow the same procedure that we followed. Hence not
 only we have to do the study in a systematic manner but also that system should be known
 to others.

 What is the value of Research?

 The nature of research problems could vary. Problems may refer to some undesirable
 situation or these may refer to simply a curiosity of the researcher that may be agitating his
 or her mind. For example, in a recent BA/BS examination of the Punjab University 67 percent
 of the students failed. That is a colossal wastage of the resources, hence an undesirable
 situation that needs research to find a solution. The researcher may come up with a variety
 of reasons that may relate with the students, the teachers, the curricula, the availability of
 books, the examination system, the family environment of the student, and many more. So,
 a study may be carried out diagnose the situation, and the recommendations to be applied to
 overcome the undesirable situation of mass failure of students.

 In the same examination result one finds that girls have captured a good number of top
 positions; and that is happening for the last couple of years. One gets curious and tries to do
 research for finding out the reasons. This is an academic problem but certainly a research
 problem. Conducting such research offers the pleasure of solving a puzzle. Why the girls
 are catching most of the top positions in different examination? This might be a puzzle that
 the research may like to explain. Such findings make a good contribution to the body of
 knowledge i.e. making some good discoveries as part of the basic research. Finding answer
 to any enigma is self-satisfying.
 The researchers try to make use of their findings for generating theories and models that
 could be used for understanding human behavior and the functioning of different structures
 both at the micro (organizational) and macro (societal) level.
        Therefore, research may be considered as an organized, systematic, data based, critical,
        objective, scientific inquiry or investigation into a specific problem, undertaken with the
        purpose of finding answers or solutions to it. In this way research provides the needed
        information that guides the planners to make informed decisions to successfully deal with the
        problems. The information provided could be the result of a careful analysis of data gathered
        firsthand or of the data that are already available with an organization.

      The value of research for policy makers, planners, business managers, and other stakeholders
      is that it reduces uncertainty by providing information that improves the decision-making
      process. The decision- making process associated with the development and implementation
      of a strategy involves four interrelated stages:

   1. Identifying problems or opportunities;
   2. Diagnosing and assessing problems or opportunities;
   3. Selecting and implementing a course of action; and
   4. Evaluating the course of action.

      Identifying problems and solutions to the same problems is in fact applying the research
      findings to overcome an undesirable situation. Initially a problem may appear to be simply a
      ‘tip of the iceberg’ but the study by a professional might help locating the magnitude of the
      issue as well as its solutions. Such research is usually referred to as applied research, which
      shall be discussed in detail in the coming lectures.

3. Classification of Research
          Four main dimensions:
      1. Purpose of doing research.
      2. Intended uses of research.
      3. How it treats time → time dimension.
      4. The research techniques used
Purpose of Research:
What the researcher trying to accomplish.
      1. Exploratory/ Formulative
      2. Descriptive
      3. Explanatory
      4. Studies can be multi-purpose
a. Exploratory Research:
      ▪     Initial research conducted to clarify and define the nature of the problem. Exploring a new
          topic.
      ▪   Specifically, there could be number of goals of exploratory research.
Goals of Exploratory Research:
      ▪   Become familiar with the topic. Develop well grounded picture of the situation.
      ▪   Develop tentative theories.
      ▪   Determine the feasibility of study.
      ▪   Formulate questions and refine issues for more systematic inquiry.
                                                                                  MUHAMMAD IMRAN     2

   ▪   Develop techniques and a sense of direction for future research
b. Descriptive Research:
    Research designed to describe characteristics of the phenomenon understudy.
    Helps in diagnostic analysis
Goals of Descriptive Research:
   ▪   Describe the situation/characteristics. Provide an accurate profile of a group.
   ▪   Give a verbal or numerical picture (%).
   ▪   Present basic background information.
   ▪   Create a set of categories or classify.
   ▪   Clarify sequence, set of stages.
   ▪   Focus on ‘who’, ‘what’, ‘when’, ‘where’ and ‘how’ but not on ‘why’.
c. Explanatory Research:
   ▪   Also called as causal research i.e.
   ▪   ‘Why’? Explanation.
   ▪   Identify cause and effect relationship among different factors.
Goals of Explanatory Research:
   ▪   Explain things not just reporting. Why?
   ▪   Which explanation is better.
   ▪   Determine the accuracy of theory.
   ▪   Advance knowledge about underlying process
   ▪   Build and elaborate a theory → complete.
   ▪   Extend a theory or principle into new areas.
   ▪   Provide evidence to support or refute an explanation or prediction.
2. Intended Uses of Research:
   a. Basic Research
   ▪   Pure/ fundamental/ academic
   ▪   Developing/ refuting/ supporting theories.
   ▪   Expand knowledge.
   ▪   Explanatory research is the most common
   ▪   Applied can also contribute.
b. Applied Research:
   ▪   Solve specific problems → help practitioners. Market new product.
   ▪   Choose one policy over the other.
   ▪   For improving productivity → problem with machines, raw material, persons working.

Basic Research

Lesson 1. INTRODUCTION, DEFINITION & VALUE OF RESEARCH

Whether we are aware of it or not, we are surrounded by research. Educators, administrators,
government officials, business leaders, human service providers, health care professionals, regularly
use social research findings in their jobs. Social research can be used to raise children, reduce crime,
improve public health, sell products, improve workers’ efficiency, or just understand one’s life.

Assume for the moment that you are the Manager of a restaurant. You are experiencing a significant
turnover in your waiter/waitress pool, and long-time customers have been commenting that the friendly
atmosphere that has historically drawn them to your door is changing. What will you do? Where will you
try to solve this problem? The problem of high turnover and decline in the friendly atmosphere at the
restaurant has to be researched.

The study of research methods provides you with the knowledge and skills you need to solve the
problem and meet the challenges of a fast-paced decision-making environment. A systematic inquiry
whose objective is to provide information to the problems (be they managerial as in our example) is one
way to explain research.

What is Research?

General image of the research is that it has something to do with the laboratory where scientists are
supposedly doing some experiments. Somebody who is interviewing consumers to find out their opinion
about the new packaging of milk is also doing research. Research is simply the process of finding
solutions to a problem after through study and analysis of the situational factors. It is gathering
information needed to answer a question, and thereby help in solving a problem. We do not do study in
any haphazard manner. Instead we try to follow a system or a procedure in an organized manner. It is
all the more necessary in case we want to repeat the study, or somebody else wants to verify our
findings. In the latter case the other person has to follow the same procedure that we followed. Hence
not only we have to do the study in a systematic manner but also that system should be known to others.

What is the value of Research?

The nature of research problems could vary. Problems may refer to some undesirable situation or these
may refer to simply a curiosity of the researcher that may be agitating his or her mind. For example, in
a recent BA/BS examination of the Punjab University 67 percent of the students failed. That is a colossal
wastage of the resources, hence an undesirable situation that needs research to find a solution. The
researcher may come up with a variety of reasons that may relate with the students, the teachers, the
curricula, the availability of books, the examination system, the family environment of the student, and
many more. So, a study may be carried out diagnose the situation, and the recommendations to be
applied to overcome the undesirable situation of mass failure of students.

In the same examination result one finds that girls have captured a good number of top positions; and
that is happening for the last couple of years. One gets curious and tries to do research for finding out
the reasons. This is an academic problem but certainly a research problem. Conducting such research
offers the pleasure of solving a puzzle. Why the girls are catching most of the top positions in different
examination? This might be a puzzle that the research may like to explain. Such findings make a good
contribution to the body of knowledge i.e. making some good discoveries as part of the basic research.
Finding answer to any enigma is self-satisfying.
The researchers try to make use of their findings for generating theories and models that could be
used for understanding human behavior and the functioning of different structures both at the micro
(organizational) and macro (societal) level.

Therefore, research may be considered as an organized, systematic, data based, critical, objective, scientific
inquiry or investigation into a specific problem, undertaken with the purpose of finding answers or solutions to
it. In this way research provides the needed information that guides the planners to make informed decisions
to successfully deal with the problems. The information provided could be the result of a careful analysis of
data gathered firsthand or of the data that are already available with an organization.

The value of research for policy makers, planners, business managers, and other stakeholders is that it reduces
uncertainty by providing information that improves the decision-making process. The decision- making process
associated with the development and implementation of a strategy involves four interrelated stages:

   1. Identifying problems or opportunities;
   2. Diagnosing and assessing problems or opportunities;
   3. Selecting and implementing a course of action; and
   4. Evaluating the course of action.

 Identifying problems and solutions to the same problems is in fact applying the research findings to
 overcome an undesirable situation. Initially a problem may appear to be simply a ‘tip of the iceberg’ but the
 study by a professional might help locating the magnitude of the issue as well as its solutions. Such research
 is usually referred to as applied research, which shall be discussed in detail in the coming lectures.

Research helps in developing methodologies

 By now we know that the researchers have to develop methodologies for carrying out the research. These
 methodologies are for the collection of data, data processing and data analysis. For the new researchers, these
 methodologies are already available, most of the researchers just use these. Nevertheless, there is always a
 scope for improvement and certainly new methodologies are developed. Also, we try to borrow methodologies
 from sister subjects.

What is the difference between a scale and index? 3
Scale:
   1. Measures intensity: Scales quantify how strongly respondents feel or experience something, like pain
       levels.
   2. Organizes on continuum: Responses are placed along a spectrum, like a Likert scale ranging from
       "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree."
   3. Single or multiple indicators: Can use one question or multiple questions to assess a concept, such as a
       happiness scale.
   4. Ordinal level: Data categorized into ordered ranks but lacks precise measurement, like ranking
       satisfaction as "low," "medium," or "high."
Index:
   1. Combines indicators: Researchers merge various measures into one score, like the Human Development
       Index.
   2. Composite score: Results in a single value derived from multiple factors, such as the Consumer Price
       Index.
   3. Reflects multiple dimensions: Represents diverse aspects of a concept, like the Poverty Index combining
       income, education, and health data.
   4. Provides holistic view: Offers a comprehensive assessment of a construct, like the Quality of Life Index.

What is scale and explain its properties 5
  1. Uniquely classifies: Each response represents a distinct level, like categorizing pain as mild, moderate, or
      severe.
  2. Preserves order: Maintains the sequence of responses, such as ranking satisfaction from lowest to highest.
  3. Equal intervals: Spaces between response options are consistent, like temperature measured in Celsius or
      Fahrenheit.
  4. Natural zero: Possesses a true absence or starting point, as in age or income.
  5. Exhaustive coverage: Encompasses all possible responses within the defined range, like rating scales from
      1 to 10.

Difference semi structure and unstructured interview
Structured interviews involve asking predetermined questions in a fixed order, ensuring consistency and
comparability. For example, a survey about customer satisfaction might include questions like "On a scale of 1 to
10, how satisfied are you with our product?" These interviews are ideal for quantitative analysis.
In contrast, semi-structured interviews blend predefined questions with open-ended ones, allowing flexibility
and deeper exploration. For instance, in a study about job satisfaction, researchers might ask about specific

aspects of the job but also encourage participants to elaborate on their experiences. This approach suits
qualitative research, enabling nuanced insights and context-rich data.
Both interview types offer distinct advantages: Structured interviews ensure uniformity in responses, aiding in
statistical analysis, while semi-structured interviews foster in-depth understanding by allowing participants to
express themselves freely. Choosing between them depends on research goals, the depth of inquiry required, and
the level of flexibility desired in engaging with participants.

Briefly Explain Qualitative Research? / Write Short Note On Quantitative Research/ Different Qualitative
And Quantitative Research With Example?
Qualitative Research: Qualitative research aims to understand social phenomena deeply, often through methods
like interviews or textual analysis. For example, a study on the experiences of cancer survivors might use
interviews to explore their emotions and coping strategies.
Quantitative Research: Quantitative research focuses on descriptive analysis and examining relationships
between variables. For instance, a survey investigating the correlation between exercise frequency and mental
health scores uses statistical analysis to quantify this relationship.

Qualitative vs Quantitative Research:
Qualitative Research:
  1. Explores social phenomena deeply through interviews, textual analysis, etc.
  2. Focuses on understanding "how" and "why" questions about phenomena.
  3. Aims for discovery and comprehension of complex social dynamics.
Quantitative Research:
  1. Analyzes variables and relationships using statistical methods.
  2. Addresses questions about the relationships between variables.
  3. Seeks verification or disconfirmation of hypotheses through deductive reasoning.

Enlist five qualitative research method. 5
Five qualitative research methods are discussed in this subject as discussed by John W. Creswell in his Book.
Following are the five qualitative research methods:

Enlist five qualitative research methods:
   1. Narrative Research: Focuses on gathering and interpreting stories or accounts to understand experiences
        deeply.
   2. Phenomenology: Explores individuals' lived experiences to uncover underlying meanings and essences.
   3. Grounded Theory: Develops theories by systematically analyzing data to uncover patterns and themes.
   4. Ethnography: Immerses researchers in a cultural context to understand social phenomena within their
        natural settings.
   5. Case Study: In-depth examination of a specific instance or situation to explore complex phenomena
        within its context.

***How many type of researches are there? 5
   • Quantitative Research: Utilizes numerical data and statistical analysis to quantify relationships and
     patterns.
   • Qualitative Research: Explores phenomena through non-numerical data to understand meanings and
     interpretations.

   •   Experimental Research: Manipulates variables to establish cause-and-effect relationships in controlled
       settings.
   •   Survey Research: Gathers data from a sample population through questionnaires or interviews.
   •   Case Study Research: In-depth analysis of a specific individual, group, or phenomenon.
   •   Observational Research: Systematic observation and recording of behavior in natural settings.

population parameters on the basis of sample observation.
3: STATISTICS (3)
STATISTIC A statistic is the summary description of a given variable in a survey sample.
Thus, the mean income computed from the survey sample and the age distribution of that

parameters.

A concept is a generalized idea about a class of objects, attributes, occurrences, or
processes that has been given a name. In other words, a concept is an idea expressed as a

relationship could be non-directional or directional, positive or negative, causal or simply
